subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
passage: Neel had six browser tabs of coding courses open, each promising to make him a programmer in thirty days. On Sunday he closed five, bookmarked one beginner Python course and stuck a note above his desk: One lesson a day. No new course until this one ends. His sister Nikita teased him when he refused to open a trending video about a shiny new language. Neel typed every example himself, then changed a number to see what would happen. Twenty-eight days later he finished the last lesson and wrote a tiny program of his own that counted the days to Nikita's birthday and printed a message. It was off by one on the first run. He fixed it without help and grinned at the screen.

qa.q: What did Neel write on the note above his desk?
qa.a: One lesson a day, and no new course until this one ends.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt when he refused the trending video?
qa.a: Tempted but determined: he held to his rule even though a new course looked exciting.

qa.q: What else could Neel do to make his practice stick, and why?
qa.a: Change each example and predict the result before running it, since testing his own guesses builds skill beyond copying.

qa.q: How does Neel's plan look to Nikita?
qa.a: Nikita sees her brother ignore the trend and stick with one course; she teases him, but may be impressed when he finishes and builds something for her.

grounding: A student picks one beginner course, sets one lesson a day, resists other courses and writes a small program of his own.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
passage:
“Raghav, there's a new course on making games. Want the link?” Swati held out her phone across the dinner table.
“Not yet, Didi. I'm on lesson nineteen of the beginner Python one.”
“You said that about the web one last month.”
“That's why I stopped it. I had four courses open and finished none. Now it's one course, one lesson every evening, and this is my proof.” He tapped a notebook page full of ticks.
“And after the last lesson?”
“Then I write something myself. Maybe a program that tells Amma which plants need water today.”
“She'll love that. So I send you the game link later?”
“Save it for me. Lesson twenty first.”
Three weeks later, a small program printed a list of thirsty plants on the laptop screen, and Swati read it aloud to Amma.

qa.q: Which lesson is Raghav on when Swati offers the game course link?
qa.a: He is on lesson nineteen of the beginner Python one.

qa.q: How does Raghav feel about the four courses he left unfinished, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He seems a little embarrassed by them and determined not to repeat it; he says that is why he stopped, and he keeps a notebook of ticks as proof.

qa.q: What else could keep Raghav going if a lesson gets dull?
qa.a: He could find a classmate doing the same course and compare progress each week, because someone expecting an update makes skipping harder.

qa.q: How might Swati see Raghav turning down the game link?
qa.a: At first it may look stubborn to her, but reading his plant program aloud to Amma shows her that finishing one course paid off.

grounding: Shows a teen sticking with one beginner Python course, a lesson each evening, parking new courses until he finishes and writes his own program.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
passage:
Last June I made myself one promise: one Python course, start to finish, no switching. I'm Manoj, and before that summer I had bookmarked eleven courses and completed zero.
I picked a free beginner course with thirty short lessons and stuck a sheet on my cupboard with thirty boxes. One lesson, one box. Around lesson twelve, Dilnaz sent me a course on building apps. She said it was much cooler. I wanted it badly. I wrote its title on the back of my sheet instead and kept going.
The loops lesson took me three evenings, so the thirty boxes took thirty-two days. The day after the last box, I still didn't open anything new. I wrote a tiny program that quizzes my little brother on spellings. Only after it worked did I click Dilnaz's link.

qa.q: How many courses had Manoj bookmarked before that summer?
qa.a: Manoj had bookmarked eleven courses and completed zero.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when Dilnaz sent the app-building course, and what was done with that feeling?
qa.a: Manoj felt tempted and wanted it badly, but stayed determined and wrote its title on the back of the sheet instead of starting it.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Manoj better if the loops lesson had stalled for a whole week?
qa.a: Asking a teacher or someone who codes for help with that one lesson would keep the single course moving, instead of letting a hard patch become a reason to switch.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see the link being saved for later?
qa.a: Dilnaz might feel briefly brushed off, but later finds Manoj has finished a course and built a working program, so the suggestion finally gets a real try.

grounding: Illustrates choosing a single beginner course, one lesson a day, setting other courses aside, and writing an own small program at the end.
